set1.q: A 39-year-old man with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis has a chest radiograph, a sputum sample sent for a rapid molecular test and a mycobacterial culture, and a tuberculin skin test placed. Which of these results is expected to take weeks?
opts: Molecular tests are the fast part of the workup: they can provide rapid results, which is why one is performed on at least one respiratory specimen. Tell: the result that takes weeks is the culture, because the organism grows slowly.
The skin test is read by a trained reader at 48 to 72 hours, measuring transverse induration in millimeters. Tell: a reading in 2 to 3 days is not the slow result; the culture is.

Chest radiography is part of the initial evaluation, and it supports suspicion but cannot confirm tuberculosis. Tell: the result that waits on slow organism growth is the mycobacterial culture, not imaging.

Correct. Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows slowly, so cultures can take weeks, while molecular tests can provide rapid results. That is why at least one respiratory specimen also gets a rapid molecular test, and why culture-based drug-susceptibility results arrive later.

set1.q: A 57-year-old woman in airborne isolation for presumed infectious pulmonary tuberculosis needs transport to radiology for computed tomography. Which measure applies during transport?
opts: Computed tomography can clarify findings or complications when needed, and transport is managed with patient source control rather than by withholding the study. Tell: precautions travel with her.
Gloves and gown for the transport team
Tuberculosis spreads by airborne aerosols, so gloves and gowns do not address the risk. Tell: the transport measure is source control for the patient, with respiratory protection for staff.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a single sputum culture that grows Mycobacterium avium complex at a routine visit. His symptoms are at baseline and no chest imaging has been done. Which best describes his status?

Correct. A respiratory isolate alone does not prove nontuberculous disease. Diagnosis requires all domains: compatible symptoms and imaging, exclusion of alternatives and usually 2 or more sputum cultures with the same species. He has one culture, no new symptoms and no imaging.

The isolate is Mycobacterium avium complex, but one culture with baseline symptoms and no imaging does not prove disease. Tell: every domain must be met, including a second culture of the same species or a qualifying lavage or biopsy.
Mycobacterium avium complex is a nontuberculous mycobacterium, not a member of the tuberculosis complex. Tell: species identification separates them, because transmission and treatment differ.

set1.q: A 40-year-old man with human immunodeficiency virus infection shares an apartment with a roommate who has infectious pulmonary tuberculosis. He has had a cough for 8 days. Which approach should be avoided?
opts: Waiting for 3 weeks of cough to evaluate

Correct. Symptoms may be mild or absent, and a high-risk patient should not wait 3 weeks to be evaluated. Human immunodeficiency virus infection is a major progression risk and close contact is an exposure risk, so symptoms or high suspicion call for disease evaluation now.
Evaluating him for tuberculosis disease now

This is the right move, not one to avoid: symptoms or high clinical suspicion require disease evaluation now. Tell: an immunocompromised close contact with a cough is exactly the patient who gets evaluated immediately.
Three sputum specimens are part of the microbiologic evaluation of suspected pulmonary tuberculosis, so they belong in his workup. Tell: the approach to avoid is delay, not testing.
Chest radiography is part of the initial evaluation, so it should be done, not avoided. Tell: imaging supports suspicion and is paired with microbiology in a high-risk contact with symptoms.

set1.q: A 46-year-old woman has newly diagnosed latent tuberculosis infection. Which item in her history most raises her risk of progressing to tuberculosis disease?
opts: Bacille Calmette-Guérin vaccination matters for testing, not progression: it can cause a false-positive tuberculin skin test, and an interferon-gamma release assay is preferred for most vaccinated patients. Tell: it is not on the list of progression risks.

Recent infection is the higher-risk timing, especially within 2 years of acquiring it. Tell: an infection picked up 15 years ago is remote, so the age of her infection is the reverse of a progression risk.

A normal chest radiograph is the usual finding in latent infection and adds no progression risk. Tell: the progression risks are immune problems (human immunodeficiency virus, transplantation, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, prolonged corticosteroids), recent infection and young age.

Correct. Tumor necrosis factor inhibitors are listed with transplantation and prolonged corticosteroid therapy among the higher risks of progression after tuberculosis infection, alongside human immunodeficiency virus infection and major immunosuppression.

set1.q: A 46-year-old man who travels for work needs testing for tuberculosis infection and says he cannot return to the clinic a second time within the next week. Which test fits his constraint?
opts: The skin test must be read by a trained reader 48 to 72 hours after placement, which means a second visit. Tell: the one-visit option is the blood test.
Sputum specimens are collected for suspected pulmonary disease, 3 of them 8 to 24 hours apart, not to test for infection. Tell: he needs an immune-response test, and the blood test needs one visit.

A radiograph is part of evaluating a positive test, but imaging cannot confirm tuberculosis and does not detect infection. Tell: testing for infection uses the skin test or blood test, and only the blood test fits one visit.

Correct. The interferon-gamma release assay needs one visit for specimen collection; it is a blood test of immune responses to tuberculosis-specific antigens. The skin test needs a return visit, because a trained reader measures it at 48 to 72 hours.

set1.q: A 42-year-old woman is in week 4 of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for pulmonary tuberculosis. Susceptibility testing shows her organism is susceptible to isoniazid and rifampin. Which change is appropriate?
opts: Pyrazinamide belongs to the full initial 2 months; the susceptibility result releases ethambutol, not pyrazinamide. Tell: at week 4 she is still inside the initial phase.
Rifampin is one of the two drugs that continue through the 4-month continuation phase, and confirmed susceptibility to it is a reason to keep it. Tell: the drug that can stop is ethambutol.

Moxifloxacin belongs to the 17-week rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen, not to the standard regimen of a patient with a susceptible organism. Tell: susceptibility allows narrowing, so a drug comes off rather than on.

Correct. Ethambutol can stop once susceptibility to isoniazid and rifampin is established. Isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide continue to complete the initial 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin continue for 4 more.

set2.q: A 61-year-old woman has untreated latent tuberculosis infection. She is about to begin prolonged corticosteroid therapy for another illness. Which complication is she now at higher risk of?
opts: Healing into a scar of nonviable organisms

Healed lesions with nonviable organisms come with increasing immunity, when the immune reaction quells the infection. Tell: corticosteroids diminish immunity, the state in which dormant foci reactivate.

Correct. Prolonged corticosteroid therapy is one of the higher progression risks, alongside human immunodeficiency virus infection, transplantation and tumor necrosis factor inhibitors. Latent infection can progress to disease, often with impaired immunity, which is the risk she now carries.
Spread of her latent infection to family

Latent infection is not infectious and does not cause transmission, whatever her immune status. Tell: the risk her steroid therapy adds is progression in her own body; transmission becomes possible if pulmonary or laryngeal disease develops.

Immunosuppression works the other way: it can cause false-negative skin tests and interferon-gamma release assays and reduces assay sensitivity. Tell: steroid therapy makes a test miss infection, not invent it.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man starts treatment for macrolide-susceptible Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease and asks how long he will need it. Which answer is accurate?
opts: Correct. Treatment continues for at least 12 months after culture conversion, so the clock starts when cultures turn negative, not with the first dose. That makes the whole course longer than 12 months.
The 12 months are counted from culture conversion, not from the first antibiotic dose. Tell: the clock waits for negative cultures, so the whole course runs longer than a year.
Symptom response does not set the duration; the regimen continues for at least 12 months after culture conversion. Tell: the anchor is the culture result, not how he feels.
Until his chest imaging is normal
Imaging does not set the duration of therapy; the regimen continues at least 12 months after cultures convert. Tell: the end point is anchored to culture conversion.

set2.q: A 63-year-old man has a chest radiograph showing fibrotic upper-lobe scarring that suggests prior tuberculosis, and he has never been treated for it. His tuberculin skin test shows 6 mm of induration. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: 15 mm applies when there are no known risk factors. Tell: a radiograph suggesting prior tuberculosis is itself a 5 mm risk, so his 6 mm is positive.
10 mm is for increased exposure risk, selected medical risks, high-risk congregate settings and children under 5. Tell: scarring that suggests prior tuberculosis belongs to the 5 mm group.
Negative; old scars cause false results

The listed causes of a false-positive skin test are bacille Calmette-Guérin vaccination and some nontuberculous exposures; false negatives come from early infection, immunosuppression or severe disease. Tell: his scarring is a 5 mm risk group, not a source of error.

Correct. Imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis places him in the 5 mm group, together with human immunodeficiency virus, recent close contact, transplant and major immunosuppression. 6 mm meets that cut-off, and his fibrotic lesion also warrants review of prior treatment and exclusion of active disease.

set2.q: A 28-year-old woman has drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis and, after expert review, is eligible for a shorter regimen. Which shorter regimen fits her?
opts: The 4-month regimen (2 months of isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide, with or without ethambutol, then 2 months of isoniazid and rifampin) is for selected children with nonsevere disease. Tell: she is an adult, well past 12.

Correct. Patients aged 12 or older with susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis can receive the 17-week rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen: 8 weeks of isoniazid, rifapentine, pyrazinamide and moxifloxacin, then 9 weeks of isoniazid, rifapentine and moxifloxacin. Eligibility needs expert review.
Weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 3 months is a latent-infection regimen. Tell: she has disease, and the shorter disease regimen is the 17-week rifapentine-moxifloxacin course.
Daily rifampin for 4 months treats latent infection, not disease. Tell: her shorter disease option keeps four drugs for the first 8 weeks.

set2.q: A 30-year-old man has latent tuberculosis infection; disease has been excluded, he takes no other medicines, and the source case's organism is fully susceptible. Which is a preferred short regimen?
opts: Correct. Daily rifampin for 4 months is one of the preferred short latent-infection regimens, along with weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 3 months and daily isoniazid plus rifampin for 3 months. Isoniazid alone for 6 or 9 months is the alternative when rifamycins are unsuitable.
Isoniazid for 6 or 9 months is an alternative, used when rifamycin regimens are unsuitable. Tell: he has no interactions or resistance concerns, so a preferred short rifamycin regimen fits.
Four drugs for 2 months, then two for 4
That is the regimen for drug-susceptible tuberculosis disease. Tell: latent infection is treated with a short preferred regimen such as 4 months of rifampin.
The 17-week rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen treats susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis disease in patients aged 12 or older. Tell: he has latent infection, which uses a latent-infection regimen.

set2.q: A 28-year-old woman shared an office with a coworker diagnosed with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis 2 weeks ago, and her exposure has now ended. She has no symptoms and no immune problem, and her interferon-gamma release assay today is negative. Which next step is most appropriate?
opts: Sputum testing is for symptoms or suspicious imaging suggesting pulmonary disease. Tell: she is symptom-free; her question is infection, answered by repeating the immune-response test later.
Latent-infection treatment is for documented infection after disease is excluded, and her test is negative. Tell: the next step is to repeat the test 8 to 10 weeks after her last exposure.
Repeat the test in 8 to 10 weeks

Correct. Early infection can produce a negative skin test or interferon-gamma release assay, so testing is repeated 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure when indicated. She is symptom-free and immunocompetent, so no immediate disease evaluation is triggered.
A negative test 2 weeks after exposure may simply be too early, because early infection can produce a negative result. Tell: the repeat test 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure is what clears her.

set2.q: A 7-year-old boy has nonsevere drug-susceptible tuberculosis and, after expert review, is a candidate for a shorter regimen. Which shorter regimen fits him?

Rifampin alone for 4 months is the latent-infection regimen. Tell: his disease needs multidrug therapy; the pediatric shorter course still starts with three or four drugs.
Weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 3 months treats latent infection. Tell: a child with disease needs the 4-month multidrug regimen, which starts with three or four drugs.

set2.q: A 74-year-old man had calcified granulomas on chest radiographs years ago and has had no new tuberculosis exposure. After months of prolonged corticosteroid therapy for another condition, he develops cough, night sweats, weight loss and an upper-lobe cavity. Which stage of tuberculosis best fits?
opts: Progressive primary disease develops soon after an initial infection when containment fails. Tell: his infection is old, marked by calcified granulomas from years ago, and the trigger is new immunosuppression, the setting of reactivation.

Latent infection is asymptomatic with no evidence of disease after clinical evaluation. Tell: cough, night sweats, weight loss and a cavity are disease, so his infection has moved past the latent stage.

Reinfection is a separate event that needs a new exposure to an infectious source. Tell: he has had no new exposure, and old granulomas plus steroid therapy point to his own latent infection reactivating.

Correct. Calcified granulomas may reflect prior infection, and prolonged corticosteroid therapy raises progression risk; reactivation is latent infection that progresses to disease, often with impaired immunity. Post-primary disease often involves the upper lobes and may cavitate, and with no new exposure, reinfection is not suggested.

set2.q: A 51-year-old man has 5 weeks of cough, night sweats and weight loss, and pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected. Which sputum collection plan is appropriate?
opts: One sample, collected at any time of day
A single specimen falls short of the 3 specimens required, and timing matters. Tell: collect 3 specimens 8 to 24 hours apart, with at least one taken early in the morning.
Two samples, collected 1 hour apart in clinic
Two specimens an hour apart are too few and too close together. Tell: the plan is 3 specimens 8 to 24 hours apart, with at least one early-morning specimen.
Three samples, 1 each week for 3 weeks
Three is the right number, but specimens are collected 8 to 24 hours apart, not a week apart. Tell: the whole set is collected within a few days, with at least one early-morning specimen.
Three samples 8 to 24 hours apart, 1 early morning

Correct. Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis calls for 3 sputum specimens collected 8 to 24 hours apart, with at least one early-morning specimen, sent for acid-fast smear and mycobacterial culture, with a rapid molecular test on at least one.

set2.q: A 52-year-old man with 5 weeks of cough, night sweats and weight loss is told he needs evaluation for pulmonary tuberculosis. He says he cannot have tuberculosis because he has never coughed up blood. Which response is accurate?
opts: Hemoptysis may occur but is not required, and nothing places it ahead of the other symptoms; persistent cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss are the usual picture. Tell: symptoms may even be mild or absent.
A normal exam would rule out tuberculosis
Physical examination has limited sensitivity, and a normal examination does not exclude pulmonary tuberculosis. Tell: neither a missing symptom nor a normal examination ends the evaluation.
Hemoptysis is not needed for the diagnosis

Correct. Dramatic hemoptysis is not required for a diagnosis of tuberculosis. Persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, reduced appetite and fatigue are the usual manifestations, and hemoptysis or pleuritic chest pain may or may not occur.
Without hemoptysis, the disease is latent
Latent infection is asymptomatic, and he has cough, night sweats and weight loss. Tell: the absence of hemoptysis does not make disease latent; his symptoms already describe possible disease.

set2.q: A 44-year-old woman has a positive interferon-gamma release assay. She also reports 5 weeks of cough, night sweats and weight loss. Which action should be avoided at this point?
opts: Correct. Tuberculosis disease must be excluded before latent-infection treatment, and a positive result requires evaluation for disease before preventive treatment. Her cough, night sweats and weight loss make disease possible, so she needs chest imaging and sputum testing first.
A positive result requires clinical evaluation and chest imaging, so a radiograph is exactly what she needs. Tell: the action to avoid is treating latent infection before disease is excluded.
Symptoms require microbiologic testing, with 3 sputum specimens 8 to 24 hours apart. Tell: testing is required; preventive treatment before excluding disease is what to avoid.
Risk history guides evaluation alongside symptoms, imaging and microbiology. Tell: taking her exposure history is good practice; starting preventive treatment now is the mistake.

set2.q: A 29-year-old man is diagnosed with latent tuberculosis infection after a normal clinical evaluation. He lives with his newborn daughter and asks whether he could pass the infection to her. Which statement is accurate?
opts: He is contagious until his treatment ends

Contagiousness comes from pulmonary or laryngeal disease releasing aerosols, not from latent infection. Tell: he is not infectious before, during or after his preventive treatment, which aims at the infection in his own body.
He can spread it through close household contact

Close contact raises exposure risk only when the source has infectious tuberculosis disease, which a person with latent infection does not have. Tell: the source in household spread is someone with pulmonary or laryngeal disease.
He is contagious when he coughs or sings

Coughing, speaking or singing releases infectious aerosols from pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis disease. Tell: latent infection has no active disease in his lungs or larynx, so he cannot spread it even when he coughs.
Latent infection does not spread to others

Correct. People with latent tuberculosis infection are infected but asymptomatic, are not infectious and cannot spread the disease; latent infection does not cause transmission. Spread comes from infectious aerosols released by pulmonary or laryngeal disease during coughing, speaking or singing.

set2.q: A 41-year-old woman who rehearses with a church choir indoors for hours each week is diagnosed with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis. She asks how she could have spread it to other choir members. Which describes how tuberculosis spreads in this setting?
opts: Risk increases with prolonged shared indoor air and poor ventilation, the opposite of a brief outdoor meeting. Tell: the choir risk comes from hours of singing together indoors.

Correct. Pulmonary and laryngeal tuberculosis release infectious aerosols during coughing, speaking or singing, and risk rises with prolonged shared indoor air and poor ventilation. A choir rehearsing indoors for hours fits that pattern.

Tuberculosis spreads through the air, as infectious aerosols from pulmonary or laryngeal disease. Tell: the exposure that matters for her choir is shared indoor air, especially when prolonged and poorly ventilated, not shared objects.

Transmission is airborne, from aerosols released while coughing, speaking or singing. Tell: the exposure risks are close contact with an infectious person and prolonged time in enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces, not touch.

opts: Daily isoniazid plus rifampin for 3 months still contains rifampin, a rifamycin. Tell: isoniazid without a rifamycin, for 6 or 9 months, avoids her drug interactions.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Isoniazid for 6 or 9 months is the alternative when rifamycin regimens are unsuitable, and checking interactions is part of choosing a latent-infection regimen. Each preferred short regimen contains a rifamycin (rifampin or rifapentine), which her medicines rule out.

set2.q: A 50-year-old woman with presumed infectious pulmonary tuberculosis is in an airborne infection isolation room. A nurse is about to enter her room. Which respiratory protection should the nurse wear?
opts: Gloves and gowns do not protect against inhaled infectious aerosols, the route of tuberculosis spread. Tell: the protection named for staff is respiratory, a fit-tested N95 or higher.
No mask if she is masked

Patient source control is used during transport, but staff entering the room still use fit-tested N95 or higher-level respiratory protection. Tell: source control for the patient does not replace staff respiratory protection.

Correct. Staff use fit-tested N95 or higher-level respiratory protection when caring for presumed or confirmed infectious tuberculosis. The organism spreads through aerosols released during coughing, speaking or singing, so the protection has to be respiratory.

Staff protection for airborne tuberculosis is fit-tested N95 or higher-level respiratory protection. Tell: source control is something applied to the patient during transport; the staff member needs a fit-tested respirator.

set2.q: A 47-year-old man moved 1 year ago from an area with high tuberculosis incidence. He has 6 weeks of productive cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss and hemoptysis, and his chest radiograph shows an upper-lobe cavity. His interferon-gamma release assay is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Residence in a high-incidence area is an exposure risk, and persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss and hemoptysis are pulmonary manifestations; post-primary disease often involves the upper lobes and may cavitate. Imaging and the blood test support the suspicion; sputum microbiology confirms it.

Lung abscess is on the differential for fever, weight loss, hemoptysis and cavitary disease, because these findings have a broad differential. Tell: his origin in a high-incidence area and his positive interferon-gamma release assay make tuberculosis the leading cause, pending sputum testing.

Lung cancer is one of the other causes of cavitary disease on the differential. Tell: fever, night sweats, recent arrival from a high-incidence area and a positive interferon-gamma release assay point to tuberculosis, which microbiology then confirms.

Nontuberculous disease is on the differential and causes chronic cough, weight loss and hemoptysis, with risk rising in bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and immune dysfunction. Tell: he has none of those, while his positive assay reflects tuberculosis-specific antigens.

set2.q: An 82-year-old woman in a long-term care home has 2 months of fatigue, weight loss and low-grade fever. A close contact in her facility was recently diagnosed with infectious tuberculosis. Her lung examination is normal. Which conclusion should be avoided?
opts: Her symptoms warrant a tuberculosis workup

This is accurate: weight loss, fatigue and fever are manifestations, and symptoms, risk history, imaging and microbiology guide evaluation. Tell: her recent close contact adds exposure risk to these symptoms.
Imaging and sputum should guide the workup
This is accurate: symptoms, risk history, imaging and microbiology guide the evaluation of possible tuberculosis. Tell: the mistake would be letting a normal lung examination end the evaluation.
A normal exam excludes pulmonary tuberculosis

Correct. Physical examination has limited sensitivity for tuberculosis, and a normal examination does not exclude pulmonary disease. Older adults may present atypically, so her symptoms, exposure history, imaging and microbiology must guide the evaluation.

This is accurate and should guide her care: children, older adults and immunocompromised patients may present atypically. Tell: fatigue and weight loss without cough can still be tuberculosis in an 82-year-old.

set2.q: A 42-year-old man with cough and weight loss has a sputum culture that identifies Mycobacterium bovis. How is this organism classified?
opts: Correct. The Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex causes tuberculosis; Mycobacterium tuberculosis is its principal human pathogen, and other members include Mycobacterium bovis and Mycobacterium africanum. Species identification matters because transmission and treatment differ from the nontuberculous mycobacteria.

The nontuberculous mycobacteria named are Mycobacterium avium complex, Mycobacterium kansasii and Mycobacterium abscessus, which are environmental species. Tell: Mycobacterium bovis sits inside the tuberculosis complex alongside Mycobacterium africanum.

Mycobacterium avium complex is a common cause of nontuberculous lung disease and is not part of the tuberculosis complex. Tell: bovis is grouped with tuberculosis and africanum; avium is grouped with kansasii and abscessus.

Slow and rapid growers are both found among the nontuberculous mycobacteria, which include many environmental species. Tell: Mycobacterium bovis is a tuberculosis complex member, and the complex's principal pathogen grows slowly.

set2.q: A 55-year-old man had a kidney transplant 2 years ago and takes anti-rejection medicines. His tuberculin skin test shows 8 mm of induration. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Correct. Transplant recipients are in the 5 mm group, together with human immunodeficiency virus, recent close contact, major immunosuppression and imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis. 8 mm meets 5 mm, so the result is positive; transplantation is also a higher progression risk.
10 mm is for increased exposure risk, selected medical risks, high-risk congregate settings and children under 5. Tell: a transplant is named in the 5 mm group, so 8 mm is already positive for him.
15 mm applies only when there are no known tuberculosis risk factors. Tell: a transplant recipient on anti-rejection medicines has a major risk, so his cut-off is 5 mm.

Immunosuppression does the opposite: it can cause false-negative skin tests, so a reaction in this man is more, not less, meaningful. Tell: the causes of a false-positive skin test are bacille Calmette-Guérin vaccination and some nontuberculous exposures.

set2.q: A 31-year-old man with no known tuberculosis risk factors has his tuberculin skin test read at 48 hours. There is 20 mm of erythema around 9 mm of transverse induration. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Positive; 20 mm is above his 15 mm cut-off
20 mm is the erythema, and erythema is not measured. Tell: the trained reader compares the 9 mm of induration, not the redness, with his 15 mm cut-off, and 9 mm falls short.
Positive; 9 mm is above a 5 mm cut-off

5 mm is the cut-off for human immunodeficiency virus, recent close contact, transplant, major immunosuppression or imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis. Tell: he has no known risk factors, so his cut-off is 15 mm.
Positive; 20 mm is above a 10 mm cut-off

This makes two errors: it reads the erythema and uses the 10 mm cut-off meant for increased exposure risk, congregate settings or age under 5. Tell: with no risk factors and 9 mm of induration, the result is negative.
Negative; 9 mm is below his 15 mm cut-off

Correct. The reader measures transverse induration in millimeters and does not measure erythema. With no known risk factors his cut-off is 15 mm, and his induration is 9 mm, so the result is negative despite the wide redness.

set2.q: A 49-year-old woman on targeted testing for tuberculosis infection has an interferon-gamma release assay reported as indeterminate. She has no symptoms. Which next test is most appropriate?
opts: Sputum testing is for symptoms or suspicious imaging suggesting pulmonary disease. Tell: she is symptom-free, so the indeterminate blood test is simply repeated or replaced by a skin test.
Repeat the assay or use a skin test

Correct. An indeterminate, invalid or borderline interferon-gamma release assay is handled by repeating the assay or using a tuberculin skin test as clinically appropriate. An indeterminate result says nothing either way about infection, so another immune-response test is needed.
Treat as negative; no further testing
Indeterminate is not negative: it is a nonresult that calls for repeating the assay or using a skin test. Tell: even a true negative leaves disease possible, and this result is not even negative.
An indeterminate result does not show infection, and even a positive one needs evaluation for disease before any treatment. Tell: repeat the assay or use a skin test first.

set2.q: A 68-year-old woman with bronchiectasis has a year of chronic cough with sputum, fatigue and weight loss. Computed tomography shows nodular bronchiectasis, alternative diagnoses have been excluded, and two sputum cultures grow Mycobacterium avium complex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis is on the differential of chronic cough and cavitary or bronchiectatic disease. Tell: her cultures identify Mycobacterium avium complex twice, the microbiologic evidence for nontuberculous disease.

Correct. Mycobacterium avium complex is a common cause of nontuberculous lung disease, and bronchiectasis raises the risk. She meets every diagnostic domain: compatible symptoms and imaging (nodular bronchiectasis), exclusion of alternatives, and 2 or more sputum cultures with the same species.

Tuberculosis is caused by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, and her cultures grew a different, environmental species. Tell: Mycobacterium avium complex is a nontuberculous mycobacterium, so the species identification decides it.

A respiratory isolate alone does not prove disease, which is why diagnosis needs every domain. Tell: she has compatible symptoms, nodular bronchiectasis, alternatives excluded and two cultures of the same species, so the criteria are met.

set2.q: A 2-year-old girl lives with her grandmother, who was just diagnosed with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis. The girl is well, and her first tuberculin skin test shows 0 mm of induration. Which next step is most appropriate?
opts: Early infection can produce a negative tuberculin skin test, so a result taken soon after exposure cannot clear her. Tell: she is a young child exposed at home, a contact group singled out for prompt public-health assessment.

When repeat testing is indicated after a recent exposure, it is done 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure, not a year later. Tell: a young child contact cannot wait; she needs prompt public-health assessment now.

The 17-week rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen treats drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis disease in patients aged 12 or older. Tell: she is 2 years old and well, with no disease found, so a disease regimen is the wrong tool.

Correct. Early infection can produce a negative skin test, so one negative result soon after exposure does not settle it. Young children and immunocompromised contacts need prompt public-health assessment, and infancy and young childhood carry a higher risk of progression after infection.

set2.q: A 36-year-old woman has tuberculosis of a cervical lymph node, with persistent painless enlargement. Chest imaging and sputum testing show no pulmonary or laryngeal disease, and no aerosol-generating procedure is planned. Her coworkers ask whether she is contagious. Which statement is accurate?
opts: She spreads it through skin contact

Tuberculosis spreads through airborne aerosols released from pulmonary or laryngeal disease during coughing, speaking or singing, not through touch. Tell: a painless enlarged neck node is extrapulmonary disease and does not release infectious aerosols.

Airborne precautions are used when pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis is possible. Tell: her imaging and sputum exclude both, and extrapulmonary disease without an aerosol-generating source is usually not infectious.

Correct. Extrapulmonary disease usually is not infectious unless there is pulmonary or laryngeal involvement or an aerosol-generating source. Her disease is confined to a lymph node, so the airborne route that spreads tuberculosis is absent.
She is infectious until treatment ends

Infectiousness comes from pulmonary or laryngeal disease releasing aerosols. Tell: lymph node disease without lung or larynx involvement is usually not infectious, so the length of treatment does not decide it.

set2.q: A 30-year-old woman who received BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) vaccine as a child has no known tuberculosis risk factors. A tuberculin skin test shows 16 mm of induration. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Indeterminate is a result category of the interferon-gamma release assay; a skin-test reading in millimeters is simply compared with her cut-off. Tell: 16 mm against her 15 mm cut-off is a clear positive.

Correct. The skin test is interpreted with the standard risk-based thresholds regardless of vaccination history. With no known risk factors her cut-off is 15 mm, and 16 mm meets it, so she needs evaluation for tuberculosis disease before any preventive treatment.

Bacille Calmette-Guérin vaccination can cause a false-positive skin test, but the reading is still interpreted with the standard risk-based thresholds regardless of that history. Tell: 16 mm meets her 15 mm cut-off, so it counts as positive.

A positive result still requires evaluation for tuberculosis disease before preventive treatment, with clinical evaluation and chest imaging. Tell: the 15 mm cut-off makes her positive; it does not let her skip the evaluation.

set2.q: A 64-year-old woman has chronic cough, sputum, fatigue and weight loss. Computed tomography shows fibrocavitary disease, alternative diagnoses have been excluded, and her sputum cultures are negative, but one bronchoalveolar lavage culture grows Mycobacterium avium complex. Which best describes whether she meets the diagnostic criteria?
opts: Imaging is one domain; diagnosis requires compatible symptoms and imaging, excluded alternatives and microbiologic evidence. Tell: her criteria are met because the lavage culture supplies the microbiology, not because of the scan.

Correct. Nontuberculous lung disease requires all domains: compatible symptoms and imaging (fibrocavitary disease here), exclusion of alternatives, and microbiology. One positive bronchial wash or lavage can meet the microbiologic criterion, even when sputum is negative.
Not met; two sputum cultures needed

Two or more sputum cultures of the same species are the usual route, but one positive bronchial wash or lavage, or a qualifying biopsy, can also meet the microbiologic criterion. Tell: her lavage culture counts.
Not met; a biopsy is required

A qualifying biopsy is one route, not a requirement; a single positive bronchial wash or lavage can meet the microbiologic criterion. Tell: her lavage result is enough with her symptoms, imaging and excluded alternatives.

set2.q: A 27-year-old woman starting work in a setting with ongoing tuberculosis transmission has a tuberculin skin test placed on her forearm. She asks when she must come back to have it read. When should a trained reader measure the reaction?
opts: 12 to 24 hours is too early; the reaction is measured at 48 to 72 hours after placement. Tell: the reading window opens 2 days after placement, so she returns 2 to 3 days later.
24 to 48 hours ends where the correct window begins. Tell: the trained reader measures at 48 to 72 hours, so a visit on the first or early second day would be too early.

Correct. A trained reader measures the reaction at 48 to 72 hours after the intradermal injection on the forearm, recording the transverse induration in millimeters, not the erythema. She must return within that window.
96 to 120 hours is past the reading window of 48 to 72 hours. Tell: the visit falls 2 to 3 days after placement, not 4 to 5.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection has 3 months of back pain, fever and weight loss. Imaging shows vertebral destruction, and she has new leg weakness. Spinal tuberculosis is suspected. Which next step is most appropriate?
opts: An interferon-gamma release assay shows infection but cannot distinguish latent infection from disease, and a negative result does not exclude disease, especially with immunosuppression. Tell: suspected spinal disease needs organ-specific specimens.

Latent-infection regimens treat infection after disease has been excluded. Tell: vertebral destruction with fever and weight loss is suspected disease, which must be assessed before any regimen is chosen.

Correct. Spinal tuberculosis presents with back pain, vertebral destruction or neurologic deficits, and extrapulmonary disease may need organ-specific specimens and urgent assessment. Her new leg weakness is a neurologic deficit, which makes the assessment urgent.

Waiting months ignores a neurologic deficit, and extrapulmonary disease may need urgent assessment. Tell: new leg weakness with vertebral destruction calls for urgent evaluation with organ-specific specimens now.

set2.q: A 50-year-old man is diagnosed with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis, and the health department is ranking his contacts. Which contact has the highest exposure risk?
opts: Office mate in a small unventilated room

Correct. Exposure risk rises with close contact with a person who has infectious tuberculosis and with prolonged exposure in enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces. Sharing a small unventilated office combines both, giving the most prolonged shared indoor air.
Neighbor who chatted with him outdoors
Risk increases with prolonged shared indoor air and poor ventilation. Tell: a short conversation outdoors has neither feature, so it carries far less exposure than shared office air.
Cousin he visited once for an hour

A single 1-hour visit is brief compared with sharing an office, and risk rises with prolonged exposure in enclosed spaces. Tell: contacts are ranked by how long and how closely they shared air, and the office mate has far more of both.

Passing someone briefly is not prolonged exposure, and prolonged shared indoor air is what raises risk. Tell: rank contacts by how long and how closely they shared enclosed, poorly ventilated air with him.

set2.q: A 48-year-old man is admitted with cough, night sweats and weight loss, and his sputum smear shows acid-fast bacilli. Infectious pulmonary tuberculosis is presumed. Where should he be placed?
opts: Pulmonary tuberculosis spreads through infectious aerosols, and risk rises with shared indoor air, so a shared ward exposes others. Tell: presumed infectious disease goes to an airborne infection isolation room.
Contact precautions with gown and gloves

Tuberculosis is airborne, spread by aerosols from the lungs or larynx, so gowns and gloves do not address it. Tell: airborne isolation and fit-tested N95 respiratory protection are what the setting calls for.
Cultures can take weeks, and waiting in a shared space exposes others to infectious aerosols. Tell: isolation starts on presumption of infectious disease, not after culture confirmation.

Correct. Presumed infectious pulmonary tuberculosis calls for an airborne infection isolation room when indicated, with fit-tested N95 or higher-level respiratory protection for staff, because pulmonary disease releases infectious aerosols during coughing, speaking or singing.
